prompt.context_jp: 「電気の供給___ 完全に止まっています」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「電気の供給___ 完全に止まっています」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this emergency report.

feedback.correct_en: This is a sudden situation report — brand-new information presented as a discovered fact, so が marks the subject neutrally.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 'the power supply' as a topic already under discussion, which feels off for an on-the-spot report. を is wrong because 止まる is intransitive here.

contrast_examples.jp: 電気は止まっているけど水は出る。
contrast_examples.en: The power is out, but the water still runs. (contrast topic)

prompt.context_jp: 「ＴＯＫＹＯ ＭＥＲ___ 都知事直轄の 医療組織です」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「ＴＯＫＹＯ ＭＥＲ___ 都知事直轄の 医療組織です」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits the governor's introduction of TOKYO MER?

feedback.correct_en: The governor is introducing/defining what TOKYO MER is — a topic statement 'As for MER, it is X'. は is standard for XはYです definitions.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like identifying which organization (answering 'which one is MER?'), not defining MER itself.

contrast_examples.jp: MERが都知事直轄の組織です。
contrast_examples.en: MER is the one that reports directly to the governor. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 「音羽先生___ ＭＥＲを 守ってくれたじゃないですか」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「音羽先生___ ＭＥＲを 守ってくれたじゃないですか」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits when praising Dr. Otowa directly?

feedback.correct_en: The speaker is making Otowa the topic ('As for you, you protected MER'), reminding him of what he did. は fits a reassuring reminder about an already-known person.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would newly identify Otowa as the one who protected MER, which doesn't match the praising/reminding tone.

contrast_examples.jp: 音羽先生は守ってくれた。
contrast_examples.en: You (Otowa) protected us, you know. (topic reminder)

contrast_examples.jp: 音羽先生が守ってくれた。
contrast_examples.en: It was Otowa who protected us. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 「喜多見君でも 慌てること___ あるのね」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「喜多見君でも 慌てること___ あるのね」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Akatsuka's teasing remark?

feedback.correct_en: With こと+ある meaning 'there are times when...', が marks the existing situation neutrally — a discovery that such moments exist.
feedback.incorrect_en: は here would require a contrast structure (〜ことはあるけど...). As a stand-alone observation, が is natural with ある.

contrast_examples.jp: 慌てることはあるけど、めったにない。
contrast_examples.en: I do panic sometimes, but rarely. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 「俺に___ あの人と同じことはできない」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「俺に___ あの人と同じことはできない」
prompt.prompt_en: Komaba admits his limits. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: 俺には sets up Komaba as the topic with contrastive nuance — 'As for me (unlike her), I can't do it.' には+は is standard for this self-limitation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 俺にが is ungrammatical. を doesn't fit because できる takes が/は for the ability-holder, not を.

contrast_examples.en: I can't do it (though others might).
I'm the one who can do it.

prompt.context_jp: 「赤塚知事___ 倒れました」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「赤塚知事___ 倒れました」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this urgent report to the command room?

feedback.correct_en: This is breaking news delivered to Komaba — brand-new, urgent information. が is standard for sudden-event reports.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Akatsuka as an already-established topic, undercutting the urgency of a flash report.

contrast_examples.jp: 知事は今、休んでいます。
contrast_examples.en: The governor is resting right now. (topic update)

prompt.context_jp: 「最終的な判断を下すの___ 厚生労働大臣です」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「最終的な判断を下すの___ 厚生労働大臣です」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Otowa's pointed statement?

feedback.correct_en: The 'nominalized clause + は + predicate' pattern frames 'the one who makes the final judgment' as the topic, then identifies it as the Minister. は is the natural choice here.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would double-mark focus awkwardly; in XのはYです cleft sentences, は is standard before the identifying predicate.

contrast_examples.en: The one who decides is the Minister. (cleft)

prompt.context_jp: 「死者ゼロを 続けてこられたのは 赤塚知事の判断___ あったからだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「死者ゼロを 続けてこられたのは 赤塚知事の判断___ あったからだ」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Komaba's reasoning?

feedback.correct_en: Inside the からだ clause, 判断がある presents the existence of her judgment as the single reason — exhaustive-listing が ('it was HER judgment that made it possible').
feedback.incorrect_en: は would detach '判断' from the reason clause and sound like topic shift, breaking the 〜のは〜からだ cleft.

contrast_examples.jp: 知事の判断があったからだ。
contrast_examples.en: It's because the governor's judgment was there.

contrast_examples.jp: 知事の判断はあったが足りなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Her judgment was there, but not enough. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 「私___ ＭＥＲを 解体するために来たんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「私___ ＭＥＲを 解体するために来たんです」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Otowa's self-introduction here?

feedback.correct_en: Otowa is contrasting himself with the other MER members being praised. 私は carries the 'I, unlike them' contrastive-topic nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: 私が would exhaustively identify him as the one who came — fitting a question like 'who came to dissolve MER?', not this self-deprecating admission.

contrast_examples.en: I (for my part) am against it.
I'm the one who's against it.

prompt.context_jp: 「白金大臣___ 元厚労省の医系技官です」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「白金大臣___ 元厚労省の医系技官です」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this TV commentator's framing?

feedback.correct_en: The speaker is making Minister Shirokane the topic and giving background about her ('As for Minister Shirokane, she was formerly...'). は fits topic + descriptive predicate.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would answer 'who is the former medical officer?' — identifying rather than describing a known figure.

contrast_examples.jp: 大臣は医系技官でした。
contrast_examples.en: The minister was a medical official (background info).
The minister is the former official (identifying).

prompt.context_jp: 「大使館から 空撮の許可___ 下りません」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「大使館から 空撮の許可___ 下りません」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this operations report?

feedback.correct_en: 'Permission' is new information being reported as not materializing — a neutral-description subject, so が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would imply contrast ('as for permission, it hasn't come, but something else has'), which isn't the situation.

contrast_examples.jp: 許可は下りたが時間がかかった。
contrast_examples.en: Permission did come, but took time. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 「二酸化炭素濃度___ 上がっています」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「二酸化炭素濃度___ 上がっています」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this emergency readout?

feedback.correct_en: Senju is reporting a newly observed change — neutral-description subject with が on 濃度.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame CO2 concentration as a pre-established topic, losing the 'something is happening right now' urgency.

prompt.context_jp: 「敷地内___ の侵入が 禁止されています」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「敷地内___ の侵入が 禁止されています」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the destination of 'entering'?

feedback.correct_en: 侵入 (entering) targets a destination; へ marks direction/goal, and へのN is a common formal noun-modifying pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks location of action, which doesn't fit 'entry INTO'. を would mark a path, not goal of 侵入.

prompt.context_jp: 「敷地内___ 入って いつもどおり 最善を尽くしてください」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「敷地内___ 入って いつもどおり 最善を尽くしてください」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits the governor's final order?

feedback.correct_en: 入る takes に for the destination entered — 'enter INTO the grounds'. This is the standard goal-marking に.
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks where an action happens, but 入る describes motion toward a goal. を would only work with 通る/出る-type path verbs.

prompt.context_jp: 「そんな状態で ずっと ＭＥＲ___ 指揮してたんだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「そんな状態で ずっと ＭＥＲ___ 指揮してたんだ」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the object of 'commanding'?

feedback.correct_en: 指揮する is transitive — it takes a direct object (MER) marked with を.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make MER the subject of commanding, inverting the meaning. に would mark the recipient, not the thing commanded.

contrast_examples.en: To give instructions to the team.

prompt.context_jp: 「人の命___ 懸かってるんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「人の命___ 懸かってるんです」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the expression that completes this plea at the embassy gate.

feedback.correct_en: 命が懸かる ('lives are at stake') is a fixed intransitive collocation — 命 is the subject, taking が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 命を懸ける is the transitive counterpart ('to risk one's life'); here Kitami isn't the one risking, he's saying lives hang in the balance.

prompt.context_jp: 「みんな同じよ ___で戦っているのは」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「みんな同じよ ___で戦っているのは」
prompt.prompt_en: The governor says everyone is fighting with their lives on the line. Choose the set phrase.

feedback.correct_en: 命懸け = 'at the risk of one's life', the standard phrase for a life-or-death commitment.
feedback.incorrect_en: 命拾い means 'narrow escape from death' (survived). 命知らず is 'reckless/fearless person', describing someone's character, not a mode of fighting.

contrast_examples.en: Protect at the risk of one's life.

prompt.context_jp: 「らしくないですよ ___なんて」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「らしくないですよ ___なんて」
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami responds to Komaba's uncharacteristic admission. Fill the blank.

feedback.correct_en: 弱音(を吐く) = 'to voice weakness/complaints'. Kitami is reacting to Komaba showing vulnerability, so 弱音なんて fits perfectly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 本気 ('seriousness') doesn't fit the chiding tone. 大声 ('loud voice') doesn't match what Komaba just did — speaking quietly about fear.

prompt.context_jp: 「だから 俺たちは___に乗る」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「だから 俺たちは___に乗る」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the idiomatic phrase: 'ride the ___ (go with the winner)'.

feedback.correct_en: 勝ち馬に乗る is the fixed idiom 'back the winning horse / side with the winner'. The chapter later references 勝ち馬 explicitly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 勝ち組 means 'the winners' as a group but doesn't collocate with 乗る. 勝ち星 means 'a win' in sports, not idiomatic with 乗る.

prompt.context_jp: 「最後に赤塚に 一矢 ___ために」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「最後に赤塚に 一矢 ___ために」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb that completes this idiom ('to get one shot back at').

feedback.correct_en: 一矢報いる is the set idiom 'return one arrow' — to strike back / get even in a small way.
feedback.incorrect_en: 返す and 打つ don't form fixed idioms with 一矢 in this sense. Only 報いる is paired with 一矢.

prompt.context_jp: 「___が命を決めます」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___が命を決めます」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose Kitami's urgent phrase meaning 'every second counts'.

feedback.correct_en: 1分1秒 is the standard set phrase for 'every minute, every second' in life-or-death medical urgency.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一瞬一瞬 means 'moment by moment' but doesn't collocate with 命を決める. 一日一日 ('day by day') is too slow a timescale for CPR.

prompt.context_jp: 「心配なのは分かりますが 今は 現場に___しましょう」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「心配なのは分かりますが 今は 現場に___しましょう」
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb: 'let's focus on the scene'.

feedback.correct_en: 集中する ('to focus/concentrate') is the natural choice for refocusing attention on the operation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 集合する means 'to gather/assemble' (physical meeting). 集計する means 'to tally/total' (numbers).

prompt.context_jp: 「___ 勇気と元気を頂きました」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___ 勇気と元気を頂きました」
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami replies to the hospital doctor's thanks. Fill the blank.

feedback.correct_en: こちらこそ ('the same from our side / no, thank YOU') is the standard polite response returning thanks.
feedback.incorrect_en: そちらこそ and あちらこそ aren't standard reciprocation phrases; こちら ('our side') is used because the speaker returns the sentiment from their own position.

contrast_examples.jp: こちらこそありがとう。

prompt.prompt_en: Otowa politely declines the offer of baked goods.

feedback.correct_en: お構いなく = 'please don't trouble yourself / don't bother' is the fixed polite refusal.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other forms aren't established polite-decline expressions; お構いなく specifically means 'no need to accommodate me'.

contrast_examples.en: Please don't go to any trouble.

prompt.context_jp: Reporting Akatsuka's collapse urgently to Komaba in the command room.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as an urgent flash report?

choices.text: 赤塚知事が倒れました。
赤塚知事は倒れました。

feedback.correct_en: Breaking news uses が to present the event as freshly discovered. The chapter uses exactly this phrasing.
feedback.incorrect_en: は treats the governor as an already-active topic and sounds like calm background update, undercutting the emergency tone.

prompt.context_jp: Kitami is pressing the embassy staff — people are dying inside.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural for Kitami's urgent push?

choices.text: 待ってる時間はありません。
待つ時間を持っていません。

feedback.correct_en: 〜時間はない is the idiomatic way to say 'there's no time to...'. The chapter uses exactly this phrasing.
feedback.incorrect_en: 時間を持っていません is a literal translation from English ('don't have time') that sounds foreign; Japanese uses 〜(する)時間がない/はない.

prompt.context_jp: The ward doctor thanks Dr. Kitami after the field-trip visit.
prompt.prompt_en: Which thanks sounds more natural in this polite workplace moment?

choices.text: 今日は本当にありがとうございます。
今日はとてもありがとうございます。

feedback.correct_en: 本当に modifies ありがとう naturally and is the standard intensifier for sincere thanks.
feedback.incorrect_en: とても doesn't collocate with ありがとう in natural Japanese; speakers say 本当にありがとう or どうもありがとう, not とてもありがとう.

contrast_examples.jp: 本当にありがとうございます。

prompt.context_jp: After hearing all the medical complications, a team member asks if there's nothing left to try.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds more natural for 'nothing we can do'?

choices.text: もう打つ手なしってことですか？
もうやる手段なしってことですか？

feedback.correct_en: 打つ手がない is the fixed idiom for 'no moves left / nothing to be done'. The chapter uses exactly this phrase.
feedback.incorrect_en: やる手段 is a literal paraphrase that no native speaker would use here; the idiomatic chunk is 打つ手.

prompt.context_jp: Akatsuka pushes back on Kitami's warning about hospitalization before the election.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural coming from Akatsuka here?

choices.text: 選挙前に入院なんかできないって。
選挙前に入院などすることができません。

feedback.correct_en: The casual 〜なんか + って quotative fits Akatsuka's intimate, exasperated tone with Kitami, matching the drama's register.
feedback.incorrect_en: The second line is grammatical but overly formal/stiff — it clashes with the private, pressing conversation between a longtime pair.

contrast_examples.en: I can't exactly go to the hospital.

contrast_examples.jp: 入院することはできません。
